The '''Congressional-Executive Commission on China''' ('''CECC''') is an independent agency of the [[U.S. government]] which monitors human rights and rule of law developments in the [[People's Republic of China]]. The commission was given the mandate by the [[U.S. Congress]] to monitor and report on human rights issues with a particular focus on compliance with the [[International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights]] and the [[Universal Declaration of Human Rights]]. Its reporting covers developments in [[Censorship in China|freedom of expression]], the right to peaceful assembly, [[Freedom of religion in China|religious freedom]], freedom of movement, freedom from [[arbitrary arrest and detention]] or torture, and the [[right to a fair trial]], among others.<ref name="HR4444">[http://www.cecc.gov/pages/general/HR4444_Title3.pdf H.R. 4444, TITLE III--CONGRESSIONAL-EXECUTIVE COMMISSION ON THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF CHINA] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110912012150/http://www.cecc.gov/pages/general/HR4444_Title3.pdf|date=2011-09-12}}</ref> The commission publishes an annual report to the [[President of the United States]] and Congress, typically in the fall of each year. It also maintains a database of prisoners of conscience, holds regular roundtables and hearings, and issues letters to other institutions concerning human rights matters.<ref name="CECC">{{Cite web|url=https://www.cecc.gov/index.php|title=Congressional-Executive Commission on China|website=www.cecc.gov|access-date=2019-05-29}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.cecc.gov/media-center/press-releases/xinjiang-chairs-ask-whether-world-bank-funding-crimes-against-humanity|title=Xinjiang: Chairs Ask Whether World Bank Funding Possible "Crimes Against Humanity"|date=August 23, 2019|website=Congressional-Executive Commission on China|access-date=2019-08-28}}</ref>

== Creation ==
The creation of the Congressional-Executive Commission on China (along with the [[United States–China Economic and Security Review Commission|United States-China Economic and Security Review Committee]]) emerged as part of negotiations for [[permanent normal trade relations]] with China upon [[China and the World Trade Organization|its accession to the World Trade Organization]].<ref name=":05">{{Cite book |last=Lampton |first=David M. |title=Living U.S.-China Relations: From Cold War to Cold War |date=2024 |publisher=[[Rowman & Littlefield]] |isbn=978-1-5381-8725-8 |location=Lanham, MD |pages= |author-link=David M. Lampton}}</ref>{{Rp|page=214}}

The commission was created in October 2000 under Title III of H.R. 4444,<ref>{{cite web |title=About |url=https://www.cecc.gov/about |access-date=20 November 2023 |website=Congressional-Executive Commission on China}}</ref> which authorizes normal trade relations with China and establishes a framework for relations between the two countries.<ref name="HR4444" />

==Work==
===Annual report===
The CECC publishes an annual report on human rights and rule of law developments in China, usually in the fall of each year, and covers issues such as freedom of expression, worker rights, religious freedom, ethnic minority rights, population planning, the status of women, climate change and the environment, treatment of North Korean refugees, civil society, access to justice, and [[Democracy in China|democratic governance]].<ref>Congressional Executive-Commission on China, [http://frwebgate.access.gpo.gov/cgi-bin/getdoc.cgi?dbname=111_cong_house_committee_prints&docid=f:61507.pdf 2010 Annual Report], 15 October 2010.</ref> The reports draw on a variety of sources, including information from human rights groups, media reports, government, and [[Chinese Communist Party]] documents.

===Prisoner database===
{{Update section|date=April 2023}}
As part of its mandate from Congress, the CECC maintains a partial database of religious and political prisoners believed to be detained in China. As of June 30, 2022, the database contained 10,645 names, of which 2,506 were believed to be detained at that time, while the remainder were released, deceased, or escaped.<ref>Congressional-Executive Commission on China, ''[https://www.cecc.gov/sites/chinacommission.house.gov/files/2022_CECC_Report.pdf 2022 Annual Report]'', 2022, p. 44.</ref> The database was created with the assistance of the [[Dui Hua Foundation]] and Tibet Information Network.<ref>Congressional-Executive Commission on China, [http://cecc.gov/pages/victims/index.php CECC political prisoner database] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111114044736/http://www.cecc.gov/pages/victims/index.php |date=2011-11-14 }}, accessed 11-13-11.</ref>

==Staff==
The commission consists of a staff of researchers and analysts and is overseen by as many as nine members each from the [[U.S. Senate]] and [[United States House of Representatives|House of Representatives]], as well as one representative each from State, Commerce, and Labor, and two other executive branch employees nominated by the President. The chair of the commission rotates between the majority parties from the House and Senate. The commission is currently chaired by Rep. [[Chris Smith (New Jersey politician)|Chris Smith]] (R-NJ).<ref name="CECC" />

On December 23, 2022, Chinese Foreign Minister [[Wang Yi (politician)|Wang Yi]] announced that Todd Stein, CECC deputy staff director, would be one of two individuals [[Chinese sanctions|sanctioned]] by China with effect from the same day. The order specified that this was in retaliation to the United States having sanctioned two Chinese officials earlier that month over [[Human rights in Tibet|human rights issues in Tibet]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.reuters.com/world/asia-pacific/china-sanctions-two-americans-over-tibet-rights-controversy-2022-12-23/|title=China sanctions two Americans over Tibet rights controversy|last=Yew|first=Lun Tian|work=[[Reuters]]|date=2022-12-23|access-date=2022-12-29}}</ref> In an emailed comment to The Associated Press, Stein said the sanction order against him did not matter in light of the "thousands of prisoners of conscience jailed by Chinese authorities."<ref>{{cite news |title=China sanctions 2 US citizens over action on Tibet |url=https://apnews.com/article/religion-china-tibet-human-rights-c12e52c935ad074ded3c51d02b2b1138 |publisher=Associated Press}}</ref>
